subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Gravitational Waves from Black Holes
description: A 60-second lesson on Gravitational Waves from Black Holes.

hook.text: When black holes merge, they send ripples through spacetime. LIGO detected these gravitational waves in 2015.

buildup.text: The waves stretch and squeeze space by less than a proton's width—yet LIGO's lasers are precise enough to measure it.

discovery.text: The first detection matched predictions from Einstein's 1915 theory. A century-old forecast finally confirmed.

twist.text: Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, and Barry Barish won the 2017 Nobel Prize. Decades of work preceded that 0.2-second signal.

climax.text: LIGO and Virgo now detect mergers regularly, building a catalog of black hole collisions across cosmic time.

punchline.text: Spacetime ripples from colliding black holes. A new way to hear the universe.

quiz.question: What did the 2015 LIGO detection confirm?
options: Gravitational waves from merging black holes, as Einstein predicted a century earlier
That black holes emit visible light during collisions
That black holes can be destroyed by gravitational waves

details.summary: When black holes spiral together and merge, they produce gravitational waves — ripples in spacetime detectable by instruments like LIGO and Virgo. The first direct detection in 2015 (GW150914) confirmed Einstein's century-old prediction and opened an entirely new way to observe the universe.
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational wave astronomy opened a new window on the universe. For the first time, we can observe events invisible to light — black hole mergers in total darkness — revolutionizing our understanding of compact objects.
takeaways: Merging black holes produce ripples in spacetime
Gravitational waves opened an entirely new observational window

faq.question: How does LIGO detect gravitational waves?
faq.answer: LIGO uses two 4-km laser interferometer arms arranged in an L-shape. A gravitational wave stretches one arm and compresses the other by less than a proton's width. The resulting laser interference pattern reveals the wave. Two detectors separated by 3,000 km confirm real signals.

faq.question: What did the first gravitational wave detection reveal?
faq.answer: GW150914 showed two black holes of 36 and 29 solar masses merging into a 62-solar-mass black hole, with 3 solar masses converted to gravitational wave energy.
